// reply: field tags shape the json output byte for byte: keys renamed
// by tag, an empty field omitted, a "-" field never emitted, a tagged
// declared struct nested in another. Reply names Status before it is
// declared, so dependency order is exercised too.
type Reply struct {
	Status Status `json:"status"`
	Count  int64  `json:"count"`
	Note   string `json:"note,omitempty"`
	Skip   string `json:"-"`
}
type Status struct {
	Code int64  `json:"code"`
	Text string `json:"text"`
}
r := Reply{Status: Status{Code: 200, Text: "ok"}, Count: 2, Skip: "never"};
assert.Equal(tb, 200, r.Status.Code);
assert.Equal(tb, "ok", r.Status.Text);

buf := bytes.NewBufferString("");
json.NewEncoder(buf).Encode(r);
assert.Equal(tb, "{\"status\":{\"code\":200,\"text\":\"ok\"},\"count\":2}\n", buf.String());

// omitempty admits the note once it is set.
n := Reply{Status: Status{Code: 404, Text: "gone"}, Note: "retry"};
buf2 := bytes.NewBufferString("");
json.NewEncoder(buf2).Encode(n);
assert.Equal(tb, "{\"status\":{\"code\":404,\"text\":\"gone\"},\"count\":0,\"note\":\"retry\"}\n", buf2.String());

// A declared name is a var typeref; a field write fills it in place.
var d Reply;
d.Note = "later";
assert.Equal(tb, "later", d.Note);
